messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Matiu was an 18-year-old project manager of Māori and Samoan background who presented after months of feeling as though ordinary life had become full of hidden danger. He had grown up in a house where his father’s drinking could turn the night violent, and the memories that stayed with him were not a complete story but disconnected pieces: the sharp smell of alcohol on his father’s breath in the hallway, the sight of his mother cornered by the kitchen door, the scrape of a bicycle left outside after he had been sent to fetch things from the shops, and the sound of shouting that seemed to arrive before he could make sense of anything else. When he tried to remember those nights, he felt he was only getting parts of what happened and the rest was missing, yet even those fragments brought back the same terror he had felt as a child. What frightened him most was how quickly the smell of alcohol in a bar or on someone’s clothes could pull him straight back into that terror, and how being alone with men, especially older men who stood too close or blocked his way, made his body react before his mind could catch up. Even seeing a bicycle leaned against a wall in the street could tighten his chest, because it carried him back to the years when he used to ride quickly home, trying to avoid what might be waiting inside.

After those memories began to surface more often, Matiu noticed that he started arranging his days around them. He avoided other people whenever he could, skipped gatherings where alcohol might be present, and increasingly smoked and drank to blunt the edge of what he was feeling. At work, where he managed small projects and had to move between sites and meetings, he found himself making excuses to stay at his desk or take routes that kept him away from crowded spaces and unfamiliar men. The old fragments of memory made these choices feel sensible to him: if his mind could not fully account for what had happened before, he reasoned that it was safer to keep his distance now. Yet the more he withdrew and relied on smoking or drinking to get through the day, the more he felt separate from other people and the less confident he became that he could handle even a normal conversation without something going wrong.

He also lived in a near-constant state of watchfulness. Matiu repeatedly checked that doors and windows were locked, especially at night, and he found himself scanning men’s faces for the slightest sign that they might harm him. Ordinary sounds made him jump in a way that embarrassed him, and he hated how easily a raised voice from another apartment or a sudden bang in the street could make him feel cornered. That sense of threat fed back into his memory: once he was on edge, the fragments of childhood violence came quicker and with greater force, and remembering them revived the same terror and bodily alarm. In those moments he became even more alert to alcohol smell, male presence, and the sight of bicycles outside shops or houses, because each one seemed to confirm that danger could appear without warning in the same places he was trying to live his life.

The more he watched for danger, the more danger seemed to appear everywhere. On his way to work, he would notice men walking behind him and cross the street; if someone nearby smelled of alcohol, he would tense and hold his breath; if a bicycle rattled past, he would feel a brief rush of dread that made the old scenes flash in his mind again. Those reactions did not settle him. They sent him back to smoking, to drinking in private, and to keeping other people at a distance, which gave him short-lived relief but left him more isolated and more convinced that something bad could happen at any moment. At home, his girlfriend had begun to notice how often he checked the locks and how quickly he retreated after social plans, and at work he was slipping into a pattern of staying quiet, avoiding eye contact, and arranging his schedule to limit contact with others.

By the time he sought help, Matiu was tired of living as if he were still a frightened child in that house. He said he wanted to stop jumping at ordinary sounds and to trust that being around men, alcohol, or even a bicycle in the street did not have to send him back into panic. At the same time, he was afraid that if he let his guard down, the missing pieces of memory would be followed by something worse, and that the terror he carried from childhood would take over his relationship and his work entirely.

violation_explanations: The vignette shows memories being activated by cues, but it does not clearly state that the memory itself causes new triggers or reminder cues to arise.
It describes threat increasing vigilance and alarm, but not that the sense of threat directly generates triggers or reminder cues.
